\paragraph{Model Collapse in Recursive Training.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024model} provided the first systematic empirical study of model collapse, showing that iteratively training on self-generated data leads to progressive loss of distributional tails.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2025strong} formalized this phenomenon theoretically, proving that collapse occurs even under optimal retraining conditions.
Subsequent work has characterized collapse through an information-theoretic lens~\cite{entropy_collapse2024}, demonstrating monotonic entropy decrease across generations.

\paragraph{Spectral Monitoring of Representations.}
Garrido et al.~\cite{garrido2023rankme} introduced RankMe, showing that the effective rank of representation matrices correlates strongly with downstream task performance without requiring labeled evaluation.
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2025} extended spectral analysis to monitor training dynamics, identifying phase transitions in learned representations.
These works establish spectral health as a reliable, low-cost proxy for representation quality---a property we exploit as our control signal.

\paragraph{Static Data Mixing Strategies.}
He et al.~\cite{he2025golden} proposed a fixed ``golden ratio'' for synthetic-to-real mixing that minimizes degradation under i.i.d.\ assumptions.
Garg et al.~\cite{garg2025mixing} provided theoretical bounds on optimal mixing proportions as a function of distribution shift.
Further empirical studies~\cite{mixing_empirical2025} have validated that even small real-data fractions substantially slow collapse.
However, all these approaches prescribe a \emph{static} ratio, ignoring the temporal dynamics: early generations may need less real data (representations still healthy), while later generations facing accelerating collapse require more.

\paragraph{Adaptive Data Selection.}
DCES~\cite{dces2026} applies curriculum-style selection to choose maximally informative training examples at each step.
ADAPT~\cite{adapt2025} prunes redundant or harmful samples based on gradient signals.
These methods address \emph{which} data to use but not \emph{when} to inject real data across a multi-generation pipeline---an orthogonal and complementary axis of control.

\paragraph{Calibration and Knowledge Preservation.}
Recent work has monitored calibration drift~\cite{calibration2025} and knowledge collapse~\cite{knowledge_collapse2025} as complementary degradation signals.
These indicators capture downstream consequences of collapse but respond later than spectral signals, which reflect geometric changes in the representation space before task metrics deteriorate.
Our contribution is the first method to close the loop: using a spectral early-warning signal to drive \emph{budget-constrained temporal allocation} of real data across recursive training generations.

cat > /root/spectral_collapse_ews/paper/related_work.tex << 'EOF'
\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse in Recursive Training.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024} provided the first systematic empirical study of model collapse, showing that iteratively training on self-generated data leads to progressive loss of distributional tails.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{strong_collapse2025} formalized this phenomenon theoretically, proving that collapse occurs even under optimal retraining conditions.
Subsequent work has characterized collapse through an information-theoretic lens~\cite{entropy_collapse2025}, demonstrating monotonic entropy decrease across generations.
A critical gap remains: existing analyses are post-hoc diagnostics, offering no mechanism for online detection or intervention during training.

\paragraph{Spectral Monitoring of Representations.}
Garrido et al.~\cite{rankme2023} introduced RankMe, showing that the effective rank of representation matrices correlates strongly with downstream task performance without requiring labeled evaluation.
SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} extended spectral analysis to monitor training dynamics, identifying phase transitions in learned representations.
These works establish spectral health as a reliable, low-cost proxy for representation quality---a property we exploit as our control signal.

\paragraph{Static Data Mixing Strategies.}
He et al.~\cite{he2025golden} proposed a fixed ``golden ratio'' for synthetic-to-real mixing that minimizes degradation under i.i.d.\ assumptions.
Garg et al.~\cite{garg2025} provided theoretical bounds on optimal mixing proportions as a function of distribution shift.
Further empirical studies~\cite{mixing2026} have validated that even small real-data fractions substantially slow collapse.
However, all these approaches prescribe a \emph{static} ratio, ignoring the temporal dynamics: early generations may need less real data (representations still healthy), while later generations facing accelerating collapse require more.

\paragraph{Data Accumulation and Recursive Stability.}
Gerstgrasser et al.~\cite{gerstgrasser2024} showed that accumulating all past real and synthetic data avoids collapse, but this treats the real/synthetic ratio as static and is inapplicable under fixed budget constraints where total real data is bounded.
Recursive stability theory~\cite{recursive_stability2025} proves that maintaining a constant real-data proportion ensures convergence in self-consuming loops, motivating the optimization of that proportion adaptively rather than fixing it a priori.
Falahati et al.~\cite{falahati2026} demonstrated that pluralistic reward curation prevents collapse even without ratio control, offering a complementary mechanism to mixing-ratio adaptation.
Data Mixing Laws~\cite{data_mixing_laws2024} optimize data mixtures by predicting language modeling performance from mixture composition, but do not address spectral health signals or synthetic-data collapse dynamics.

\paragraph{Adaptive Data Selection.}
DCES~\cite{dces2026} uses intra-cluster dispersion to adaptively rebalance center-edge sampling ratios within the synthetic pool, tested on GPT-2, Qwen, and OPT-6.7B across 10 rounds. Key distinction: DCES adapts sample selection \emph{within} the synthetic data, while we adapt the global real/synthetic mixing ratio based on spectral health.
ADAPT~\cite{adapt2025} uses meta-gradients to learn task sampling proportions under explicit token budgets for multi-task instruction tuning. It demonstrates budget-constrained adaptive allocation but addresses multi-task domain mixing rather than real/synthetic collapse prevention.

\paragraph{Calibration and Knowledge Preservation.}
Recent work has monitored calibration drift~\cite{calibration2025} and knowledge collapse~\cite{knowledge_collapse2025} as complementary degradation signals.
Whether spectral indicators or calibration metrics provide earlier warning of collapse remains an open empirical question that our experiments aim to investigate.
Our contribution is the first method to close the loop: using a spectral early-warning signal to drive \emph{budget-constrained temporal allocation} of real data across recursive training generations.
EOF
